key_points.point: AI experts hold a significantly more positive outlook on the impact of AI on the U.S. over the next 20 years compared to the general public. This belief is grounded in the expectation that AI will drive productivity and economic benefits. The data shows 56% of experts view the impact as positive, versus 17% of the public, suggesting a belief in the structural benefits of the technology.
key_points.verbatim: Fully 56% of AI experts surveyed say AI will have a very or somewhat positive impact on the United States over the next 20 years. This compares with 17% among the general public.

key_points.point: AI experts overwhelmingly believe that AI will provide personal benefits, with 76% stating it is more likely to benefit them than harm them. This reflects a professional optimism regarding AI's utility as a tool for productivity and advancement. The data suggests that those closest to the technology's development maintain a positive outlook on its integration into their own lives.
key_points.verbatim: Thinking about yourself, do you think the increased use of artificial intelligence (AI) is more likely to... Benefit you than harm you 76
key_points.excerpt_context: Page 82, Views of personal benefit versus harm from AI, among AI experts

key_points.point: AI experts emphasize the utility of AI in automating repetitive and mundane tasks to save time and improve efficiency. This aligns with the accelerationist goal of leveraging AI as a force multiplier for human productivity. The document notes that experts see these applications as a primary source of excitement regarding AI's potential.
key_points.verbatim: I think broadly some of the things that excite me are things like applications that can save people a lot of time from repetitive and mundane tasks. So I think automating some of those workflows.

key_points.point: AI experts express significant optimism regarding the personal benefits of AI, with 76% stating they are more likely to benefit than be harmed. This reflects a belief in the positive trajectory of AI development and its capacity to improve individual outcomes, contrasting sharply with the public's more cautious outlook.
key_points.verbatim: In contrast, the AI experts we surveyed are widely optimistic: 76% of experts surveyed say AI is more likely to benefit them

key_points.point: Experts are significantly more likely than the public to believe AI will enhance human productivity. This reflects a belief that AI acts as a force multiplier for human capability, which is a core tenet of accelerationist optimism regarding technological progress.
key_points.verbatim: Experts and the public are far apart on AIÆs potential impact on human productivity: 74% of AI experts surveyed think itÆs extremely or very likely that AI will make humans more productive over the next 20 years, compared with 17% of the general public.

key_points.point: Both the public and AI experts express significant concern regarding the current state of AI governance. There is a shared consensus that government regulation is currently too lax, indicating a perceived failure in existing oversight mechanisms to mitigate potential risks.
key_points.verbatim: Both the public and experts largely worry the U.S. government will not go far enough in regulating AI. About six-in-ten U.S. adults and 56% of experts surveyed say theyÆre more concerned about this than about the government going too far.

key_points.point: There is a profound lack of confidence in the ability of private companies to develop and deploy AI responsibly. This skepticism is particularly acute among experts in academic settings, suggesting that the current industry-led development model lacks sufficient accountability.
key_points.verbatim: 59% of the public and 55% of surveyed experts have not too much or no confidence in U.S. companies to develop and use AI responsibly.

key_points.point: Both the public and AI experts express a strong desire for more government regulation, specifically fearing that current efforts are too lax. This reflects a safetyist intention to prioritize robust oversight and guardrails to mitigate the risks associated with rapid AI deployment.
key_points.verbatim: The public and experts surveyed both more commonly say they are concerned that the U.S. government will not go far enough in regulating AI, rather than going too far.

key_points.point: There is widespread concern among both experts and the public regarding the potential for AI to facilitate misinformation at scale. This belief highlights the safetyist concern that AI capabilities can be weaponized or misused, necessitating proactive alignment and control measures.
key_points.verbatim: But I think the main issue with AI and misinformation is that you can now do misinformation at scale, at a way larger scale.

key_points.point: The general public expresses higher levels of concern regarding AI's potential to cause major harm to humans compared to experts. This reflects a safetyist perspective that prioritizes the mitigation of catastrophic or existential risks over the potential for productivity gains.
key_points.verbatim: The belief that AI will cause major harm to humans is more common among the public than AI experts. U.S. adults are more likely than experts to believe AI will cause major harm to humans (35% vs. 20%).

key_points.point: There is a shared concern among both experts and the public regarding the negative impact of AI on elections and journalism. This aligns with the safetyist intention to proactively identify and mitigate societal disruption before it becomes irreversible.
key_points.verbatim: AI experts and the public are both wary of AIÆs role in politics and journalism. Just 11% of experts surveyed and 9% of the public believe AI will positively impact elections in the U.S. over the next 20 years.

key_points.point: There is significant concern among both the public and experts regarding the potential for AI to cause major harm. While experts are generally more optimistic about personal benefits, a substantial portion of the public (43%) feels that AI is more likely to harm them than benefit them. This highlights a divergence in risk perception between the general population and the technical community.
key_points.verbatim: Thinking about yourself, do you think the increased use of artificial intelligence (AI) is more likely to... Harm you than benefit you 43
key_points.excerpt_context: Page 83, Views of personal benefit versus harm from AI, among the U.S. public

key_points.point: The public remains deeply anxious about AI-driven labor displacement, with a majority believing it will lead to fewer jobs over the next two decades. While experts are more optimistic, there is common ground in identifying specific occupations, such as cashiers and factory workers, as being at high risk.
key_points.verbatim: In our current survey, 64% of the public thinks AI will lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years.

key_points.point: Bias in AI decision-making is a significant concern shared by both the public and experts. There is a recognition that current design processes often fail to account for the perspectives of women and minority groups, leading to concerns about systemic discrimination.
key_points.verbatim: Bias in decisions made by AI is also a concern for experts and the public (55% each say theyÆre highly concerned).
key_points.excerpt_context: AI-related concerns, bias and representation, page 13

key_points.point: Experts express a nuanced, ambivalent stance toward regulation, acknowledging the need for guardrails while simultaneously fearing that excessive regulation could stifle innovation and competitiveness. This reflects a desire to balance safety with the practical realities of technological development.
key_points.verbatim: So I’m on both sides of this. I think we need to have limited regulations so that we can innovate and we can compete, because if we regulate too much, we’re going to be left behind — [but] for us not to have guardrails around [AI], to me, is wild.

key_points.point: The document highlights that AI models trained on internet-scraped data inherently reflect the biases of wealthy Western countries. This skeptic belief emphasizes that bias is not necessarily the result of malicious intent but is an unintentional, systemic product of the data sources themselves.
key_points.verbatim: So it’s a misconception that there is a malicious computer scientist embedding racism and sexism into the model. It’s completely unintentional. It’s essentially a product of ignorance of the data sources and the biases that are inherent in where we web-scrape the data from.

key_points.point: There is widespread public anxiety regarding AI-driven job displacement, with 64% of U.S. adults predicting fewer jobs in the next 20 years. This reflects the skeptic belief that AI integration will lead to measurable labor market harms and economic instability.
key_points.verbatim: Overall, 64% of U.S. adults say that over the next 20 years, AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S., while just 5% think it will lead to more jobs.

key_points.point: Experts and the public agree that AI will likely harm the integrity of elections and news, challenging the notion that AI is inherently beneficial for democratic governance. This skepticism highlights the potential for AI to erode social value and trust.
key_points.verbatim: In fact, 61% of these experts believe AI will harm elections in the future, with 50% of the public saying the same. News is also an area where small shares of experts (18%) and the public (10%) believe it will be a good thing for the country.

key_points.point: The document asserts that AI experts perceive a significant disparity in how well AI design accounts for the perspectives of different demographic groups. Specifically, experts believe White and male perspectives are well-represented, while Black and Hispanic perspectives are significantly under-represented in AI design processes. This empirical finding highlights a systemic bias in the AI development pipeline as perceived by those within the field.
key_points.verbatim: How representation of Black adultsÆ perspectives in AI design is viewed, among AI experts... Very/Somewhat well 27... Not too/ Not at all well 52

key_points.point: The document provides empirical evidence that AI experts and the general U.S. public hold divergent views on the future impact of AI. While a majority of AI experts (56%) view the future impact of AI on the U.S. as positive, only 17% of the general public shares this optimism, with 35% of the public viewing the impact as negative. This suggests a significant disconnect between the expert community's outlook and public sentiment.
key_points.verbatim: Future impact of AI on the U.S., among AI experts... Positive 56... Future impact of AI on the U.S., among the U.S. public... Positive 17... Negative 35

key_points.point: The public expresses significant concern regarding bias in AI decision-making, with 55% of U.S. adults being extremely or very concerned. This reflects a widespread skepticism about the fairness of automated systems. The data indicates that the public does not trust AI to be inherently neutral or equitable.
key_points.verbatim: When it comes to artificial intelligence (AI), how concerned are you about... Bias in decisions made by AI... Extremely concerned 29 Very concerned 26

key_points.point: There is a strong public perception that AI design fails to account for the perspectives of women. Only 27% of U.S. adults believe designers take women's views into account 'very' or 'somewhat' well, compared to 42% for men. This suggests a perceived gender bias in the development pipeline.
key_points.verbatim: How representation of womenÆs perspectives in AI design is viewed, among the U.S. public... Very/Somewhat well 27
